analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal task force to investigate and recommend action against price gouging.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 2024, referred to three House committees, and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stand up a joint task force drawing on the Justice Department, the Federal Trade Commission, and the Department of Agriculture to investigate unfair, deceptive, or fraudulent business practices that raise prices for American families. It would focus on consolidation in the food sector and manipulation of food prices across the supply chain. The task force would report to Congress every 90 days with legislative recommendations, but it would not itself impose fines or price limits.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers, especially households squeezed by grocery prices, would benefit from closer federal scrutiny of companies accused of using market power to inflate food prices. Farmers and small food producers could also benefit from recommendations targeting consolidation and input-cost analysis, since the task force must analyze costs to producers, manufacturers, and retailers.

how_it_helps.text: The task force must investigate and publish recommendations for strengthening interagency efforts against anti-competitive, unfair, deceptive, or fraudulent practices that increase prices for families.
The task force must examine consolidation in the food sector and actions to counteract food price manipulation throughout the supply chain.
It must report to Congress within 180 days of enactment and every 90 days after, covering federal spending effects on food prices and input costs for producers, manufacturers, and retailers.

analysis.who_pays: Food and agriculture companies, particularly large processors, retailers, and any firms using market power to raise prices, would bear the cost of investigation, regulatory attention, and potential future legislation the task force recommends. Taxpayers would fund the task force's work.

drawbacks.text: The task force is advisory only: it can investigate and publish recommendations, but it has no power to cap prices, fine companies, or enforce anything on its own, so its real-world effect depends entirely on Congress acting later.

Critics of anti-price-gouging measures argue that grocery inflation stemmed mainly from supply-chain and input-cost shocks, not price-fixing, and that the bill's own mandate to analyze input costs concedes that higher producer and retailer costs may be a major cause.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit to consumers is real but indirect: the bill creates an investigative body, not an enforcement tool or price limit, so families would see no immediate relief. The cost to the food industry is likewise mostly scrutiny rather than rules. As a first step toward possible legislation against food-sector consolidation, the design is reasonable; as a standalone fix for high prices, it is deliberately modest.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary, Agriculture, and Energy and Commerce committees, then to a Judiciary subcommittee, and died there with no hearing or vote before the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Angie Craig introduced the bill on May 22, 2024, and it was referred to the Committees on the Judiciary, Agriculture, and Energy and Commerce.
Two days later, on May 24, 2024, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce.
No further action was recorded before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large food and agriculture companies avoided the federal investigation into consolidation and price manipulation the task force would have conducted, and no one bore the cost of the task force's work. Consumers gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Angie Craig
for.role: U.S. Representative, Minnesota's 2nd District; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its sole sponsor.

against.name: House Judiciary, Agriculture, and Energy and Commerce Committees
against.role: Committees to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill; it received no hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Only two members were involved: the Democratic sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, with no votes taken, so no partisan pattern was ever tested.

industries.industry: Large food processors, meatpackers, and grocery retailers
industries.note: The task force would specifically investigate consolidation in the food sector and manipulation of food prices across the supply chain, putting these firms under DOJ, FTC, and USDA scrutiny. Consumers facing inflated grocery prices would be the intended beneficiaries.
The task force must analyze input costs for producers and recommend steps to prevent food-sector consolidation, which affects producers squeezed between concentrated suppliers and buyers.
